When Repayments Become a Struggle

What to do first, in what order, and the free UK services that will act on your behalf. Priority debts come before everything else.

If you're reading this because the payments have stopped adding up, two things are worth saying before anything else.

Free help exists, it's good, and it isn't the same as the companies that advertise. And acting early gives you materially better options than acting late. Almost everything below works better this month than next.

First: separate priority debts from the rest

This is the step that changes outcomes, and it isn't intuitive, because the creditors who chase hardest are usually not the ones who matter most.

Priority debts — pay these first, always. The consequences of not paying are losing your home, losing your energy supply, or court action:

  • Mortgage or rent
  • Council tax
  • Gas and electricity
  • Court fines
  • Child maintenance
  • Income tax, VAT and National Insurance
  • TV licence

Non-priority debts — still serious, but the consequences are financial rather than existential: credit cards, personal loans, overdrafts, catalogues, buy now pay later, most other unsecured borrowing.

Credit card companies phone daily. Councils and mortgage lenders often don't. It's easy to end up paying the loudest creditor while arrears build with the one who could take your home. Pay priority debts first, even while non-priority creditors are shouting. A free adviser will tell you exactly this, and will tell your other creditors so on your behalf.

Second: talk to your mortgage lender before you miss a payment

Lenders are required to treat customers in financial difficulty fairly, and they have a range of options they can apply — but nearly all of them are easier to arrange before arrears than after:

  • A temporary reduction in payments
  • A switch to interest-only for a period
  • Extending the term to lower the monthly payment
  • A payment holiday, in some circumstances
  • Adding arrears to the balance

Possession is a last resort, and lenders have to show they've explored the alternatives first. But the conversation goes much better when you start it yourself. If you've already fallen behind, it's still worth having — just have it today.

Third: get free advice, from one of these

All of these are free, impartial, and will deal with creditors for you. None will charge you a fee, and none of them needs to.

  • StepChange — the largest UK debt charity. Full debt advice and managed plans.
  • National Debtline — free advice by phone and webchat, with excellent written guides and template letters.
  • Citizens Advice — face-to-face help locally, and the strongest option if your situation involves benefits, housing or employment as well as debt.
  • MoneyHelper — government-backed guidance and a directory of regulated advisers.
  • Mind — because debt and mental health run together far more often than either gets discussed, and either one makes the other harder.

Be careful who you call. Search results for debt help are full of commercial firms charging for what the charities above do free, and some steer people toward solutions that suit the firm best rather than the person. If a service asks for a fee, stop, and call one of the five above instead.

Breathing Space

In England and Wales the Debt Respite Scheme — usually called Breathing Space — gives you up to 60 days during which most interest, fees and enforcement action stop, while you get advice and make a plan. There's a longer version for people receiving mental health crisis treatment.

You apply through a debt adviser rather than directly, which is another reason the first call should be to one of the organisations above. Scotland has its own statutory moratorium under the Debt Arrangement Scheme.

What not to do

  • Don't borrow to pay debt without proper advice first. It's the instinct, and it usually makes things worse, particularly if it means securing previously unsecured debt against your home. See what that actually changes.
  • Don't ignore court paperwork. A claim form isn't the end of anything — responding is free and preserves every option. Ignoring it produces a judgment by default, which is how an unsecured debt can eventually become a charge on your house.
  • Don't pay a fee for debt advice. There's no version of this worth paying for that the charities don't do better.
  • Don't prioritise the loudest creditor. Priority debts first. See above.
  • Don't cancel your home or buildings insurance to save money if you have a mortgage. It's usually a condition of the loan, and an uninsured loss would be catastrophic.

The order, in one list

  1. Work out your actual income and essential outgoings. Honestly, on paper.
  2. Sort your debts into priority and non-priority.
  3. Contact your mortgage lender or landlord, and your council. Today, not after the next missed payment.
  4. Call one of the five free services. Let them contact the non-priority creditors.
  5. Ask your adviser about Breathing Space.
  6. Don't sign anything, and don't borrow anything, until you've had that conversation.

This is a much more common situation than it feels like from inside it, the services above deal with it every day, and it's fixable. The hardest part is the first phone call.
